summary: This work demonstrates single-photon counting with superconducting microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKIDs) across the mid-infrared from 3.8 to 25 µm, achieving energy resolving powers $E/\delta E$ of 9.9, 5.9, 3.2, and 3.3 respectively with dark count rates of 4, 8, 34, and 48 mHz. Membrane-suspended aluminum detectors reach phonon-loss-limited performance at 3.8 µm, more than doubling performance versus solid-substrate devices.
motivation: Direct spectroscopy of exoplanet atmospheres in the mid-IR requires single-photon detectors with near-zero dark counts, but conventional HgCdTe and InAs/GaSb semiconductors cannot meet these demands across the full mid-IR band.
method: A 27-element MKID array with NbTiN interdigitated capacitor and aluminum central line suspended on a $\sim$100 nm SiN membrane was operated in a dilution refrigerator at 100 mK. Separate cryogenic and external optical setups with bandpass and neutral density filters provided wavelength-selective illumination; single-photon pulses were detected via optimal filtering and pulse-height analysis to extract energy resolving power.
result: At 3.8 µm the intrinsic energy resolution matches the phonon-trapping-limited prediction ($R_i = R_{\mathrm{phonon}}$ for membranes with $J=0.38$), validating the $\sim$2.4× improvement over solid substrates. At longer wavelengths (8.5–25 µm), indirect photon absorptions in the ground plane and residual far-IR background limited resolving power; optimization of lens-absorber coupling and cryogenic filtering could recover phonon-limited performance across the band.
